facts.statement: The only known specimen of Proceratosaurus is a mostly complete skull with a lower jaw and hyoid bone found near Minchinhampton in Gloucestershire.
facts.quote: The holotype and only known specimen consists of a mostly complete skull with an accompanying lower jaw and a hyoid bone, found near Minchinhampton, a town in Gloucestershire.

facts.statement: Proceratosaurus was first described in 1910 and reclassified into its own genus in 1926.
facts.quote: It was originally described in 1910 as a species of Megalosaurus, M. bradleyi, but was moved to its own genus, Proceratosaurus, in 1926.

facts.statement: The fossil was discovered by F. Lewis Bradley and described by Arthur Smith Woodward in 1910.
facts.quote: In 1910, the British palaeontologist Arthur Smith Woodward reported a partial skull of a theropod dinosaur, discovered some time prior by F. Lewis Bradley during excavation for a reservoir in the vicinity of Minchinhampton, a town in South West England.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen has been housed at the Natural History Museum in London since 1942.
facts.quote: Since 1942, the skull has been housed at the Natural History Museum in London, where it is catalogued as specimen NHMUK PV R 4860.

facts.statement: Oliver Rauhut and colleagues re-described the skull in 2010.
facts.quote: The skull was re-described by the German palaeontologist Oliver Rauhut and colleagues in 2010

facts.quote: Proceratosaurus ( ) is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived during the Middle Jurassic in what is now England.

facts.statement: The skull is 26.9 cm long and the dinosaur is estimated to be around 3 meters in length.
facts.quote: A small to medium-sized dinosaur, the skull of Proceratosaurus is 26.9 cm long as preserved, and the dinosaur is estimated to have measured around 3 m in length.

facts.statement: Proceratosaurus is classified as a coelurosaur in the family Proceratosauridae.
facts.quote: Proceratosaurus is considered a coelurosaur, specifically a member of the family Proceratosauridae

facts.statement: Proceratosaurus was likely a carnivore that ate relatively small prey.
facts.quote: Proceratosaurus is thought to have been a carnivore, with its diet probably consisting of relatively small prey.

facts.statement: The cranial crest of Proceratosaurus was likely used for display.
facts.quote: The crest was probably used for display.

facts.statement: Fossils of Proceratosaurus are found in the White Limestone Formation or the Forest Marble Formation of the Great Oolite Group in England.
facts.quote: The dinosaur is known from the Great Oolite Group of England, having been found in either the White Limestone Formation or the Forest Marble Formation.

facts.statement: It was debated whether Piveteausaurus divesensis belonged to Proceratosaurus, but later research rejected this suggestion.
facts.quote: In 1988, American paleontologist Gregory S. Paul considered the much larger theropod species Piveteausaurus divesensis from the Middle-Late Jurassic of France to belong to Proceratosaurus, coining the new combination Proceratosaurus divesensis. However, later researchers, including Rahut and colleagues in their 2010 redescription, rejected this suggestion, finding the two species to be unrelated.

facts.statement: The only known skull of Proceratosaurus measures 26.9 cm in length as preserved.
facts.quote: The only known skull of Proceratosaurus is 26.9 cm long as preserved.

facts.statement: A 2010 redescription estimated the holotype individual of Proceratosaurus to be 2.98 to 3.16 meters long and weigh between 28 and 36 kilograms.
facts.quote: The 2010 redescription considered it a small to medium-sized dinosaur, and estimated a total body length of 2.98 - 3.16 m and a body mass of 28 - 36 kg for the holotype individual

facts.statement: Other sources have estimated the length of Proceratosaurus to be between 3 and 4 meters and its body mass to be between 50 and 100 kilograms.
facts.quote: Other sources gave estimates of 3 - 4 m in length and 50 - 100 kg in body mass.

facts.statement: The infratemporal fenestra of Proceratosaurus is narrow, elongate, kidney-shaped, and around 5.4 cm tall.
facts.quote: The infratemporal fenestra is narrow and elongate, being around 5.4 cm tall and kidney-shaped

facts.statement: The mandible of Proceratosaurus is 26 cm long, which is somewhat shorter than the skull, an unusual trait for theropods.
facts.quote: The mandible (lower jaw) of Proceratosaurus is 26 cm long, somewhat shorter than the skull, which is unusual for theropods.

facts.statement: Proceratosaurus had around 4 teeth in each premaxilla, 22 in each maxilla, and 20 in each dentary.
facts.quote: each premaxilla had around 4 teeth, each maxilla had around 22 teeth, and each dentary had around 20 teeth.

facts.statement: The teeth of Proceratosaurus are heterodont, showing morphological differences depending on their position in the jaw.
facts.quote: The teeth are heterodont, showing differences in morphology depending on their position in the jaw.

facts.statement: The premaxillary teeth of Proceratosaurus are D-shaped in cross-section with an arched front-facing surface.
facts.quote: The premaxillary teeth are D-shaped in cross-section, with the front facing surface of the teeth being arched.

facts.statement: The three frontmost pairs of teeth in the lower jaw of Proceratosaurus are procumbent, protruding forwards.
facts.quote: The three frontmost pairs of teeth of the lower jaw are procumbent, that is they protrude forwards.

facts.statement: Based on related tyrannosauroids, it is reasonable to infer that Proceratosaurus was covered in simple feathers similar to modern bird down.
facts.quote: Well preserved fossils of the related tyrannosauroids Yutyrannus and Dilong indicate that they were covered in relatively simple feathers in life, similar to the down feathers of modern birds, and according to British paleontologist Dave Hone "it is reasonable to infer" that all tyrannosauroids had similar feathers.

facts.statement: Proceratosaurus was originally classified as a species of Megalosaurus in a 1910 description by Woodward.
facts.quote: Woodward classified Proceratosaurus as a species of Megalosaurus in his 1910 description

facts.statement: In the 1930s, von Huene suggested that Proceratosaurus was closely related to Ceratosaurus and considered both to be members of Coelurosauria.
facts.quote: Studies during the 1930s by von Huene suggested a closer relationship with Ceratosaurus, and he thought both dinosaurs represented members of the group Coelurosauria.

facts.statement: In 1988, Paul suggested that Proceratosaurus was a close relative of Ornitholestes, primarily due to the presence of a nasal crest.
facts.quote: Paul suggested in 1988 that it was a close relative of Ornitholestes, again mainly because of the crest on the nose

facts.statement: A 1998 phylogenetic analysis by Thomas R. Holtz Jr. classified Proceratosaurus as a basal coelurosaur.
facts.quote: A 1998 phylogenetic analysis by American paleontologist Thomas R. Holtz Jr. found Proceratosaurus to be a basal coelurosaur.

facts.statement: A 2010 study by Oliver Rauhut and colleagues concluded that Proceratosaurus was a coelurosaur and specifically a tyrannosauroid.
facts.quote: The first major re-evaluation of Proceratosaurus and its relationships was published in 2010 by Oliver Rauhut and colleagues. Their study concluded that Proceratosaurus was in fact a coelurosaur, and moreover a tyrannosauroid

facts.statement: Rauhut and colleagues named the clade containing Proceratosaurus and Guanlong Proceratosauridae, defined as theropods closer to Proceratosaurus than to Tyrannosaurus, Allosaurus, Compsognathus, Coelurus, Ornithomimus, or Deinonychus.
facts.quote: They named the clade containing these two dinosaurs Proceratosauridae, defined as all theropods closer to Proceratosaurus than to Tyrannosaurus, Allosaurus, Compsognathus, Coelurus, Ornithomimus, or Deinonychus.

facts.statement: Proceratosaurus is currently considered the oldest known tyrannosauroid, alongside Kileskus.
facts.quote: Proceratosaurus is currently the oldest known tyrannosauroid, along with Kileskus, which is known from equivalently aged rocks in Western Siberia.

facts.statement: Proceratosaurus is closely related to the tyrannosauroid Guanlong from the Late Jurassic of China.
facts.quote: Proceratosaurus was most closely related to the tyrannosauroid Guanlong from the Late Jurassic of China.

facts.statement: Proceratosaurus possessed unique "D-shaped" premaxillary teeth characteristic of tyrannosauroids.
facts.quote: Proceratosaurus also possessed the characteristic "D-shaped" premaxillary teeth that are unique to tyrannosauroids.

facts.statement: A 2023 study created a virtual composite model of a complete Proceratosaurus skull using data from Proceratosaurus and Guanlong skulls.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Proceratosaurus likely fed on small-bodied prey based on its low bite force and skull morphology.
facts.quote: The low bite force in combination with the morphology of the skull suggests that Proceratosaurus most likely fed on small-bodied prey.

facts.statement: Rauhut and colleagues suggest that the prominent head crest of Proceratosaurus was likely used as a display feature.
facts.quote: According to Rauhut and colleagues, the prominent head crest of Proceratosaurus was also likely to have been used as a display feature.
